analysis.research_question_and_background: The study aimed to address the high incidence of HBV-related hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) in China and evaluate the impact of interferon (IFN) therapy versus nucleos(t)ide analogs (NAs) on HCC occurrence in high-risk patients.
analysis.study_design_and_population: A retrospective cohort study was conducted on 368 patients with high risk of HBV-related HCC, with 120 patients receiving IFN therapy (with or without NAs) and 248 patients receiving NA therapy alone.
analysis.methods: Patients were enrolled and followed for a 5-year treatment period. HCC incidence was monitored and compared between the IFN group and the NAs group using statistical analysis to determine significance.
analysis.main_results: After 5 years of treatment, the HCC incidence in the IFN group was 2.54%, while the NAs group had a significantly higher incidence of 25.74% (P < 0.001).
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The authors interpreted these findings as evidence that IFN-based therapy significantly reduces HCC risk compared to NAs alone in high-risk HBV patients, highlighting a novel therapeutic approach.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: These results suggest that IFN-based therapy could be a more effective option for reducing HCC incidence in patients at high risk of HBV-related HCC, potentially informing treatment guidelines and public health strategies.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study is limited by its retrospective design and potential for confounding factors, but the evidence is strong due to the clear comparison between IFN and NAs groups and the statistically significant results.

analysis.summary_en: This study investigated the impact of interferon (IFN) therapy versus nucleos(t)ide analogs (NAs) on hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) incidence in patients at high risk of HBV-related HCC. The research aimed to address the high prevalence of HBV-related HCC in China and evaluate therapeutic efficacy. A retrospective cohort study enrolled 368 patients, with 120 receiving IFN therapy and 248 receiving NA therapy alone. After 5 years, HCC incidence was 2.54% in the IFN group and 25.74% in the NAs group (P < 0.001). The authors concluded that IFN-based therapy significantly reduces HCC risk compared to NAs alone, offering a novel therapeutic approach. These findings may inform treatment guidelines for high-risk HBV patients. The study's retrospective design introduces potential limitations, but the results are robust due to the clear comparison and statistical significance.

title: Knowledge, Attitude, and Practice towards Hepatitis B Infection and Vaccination among Undergraduate Students of Al-Hikmah University, Ilorin, Nigeria
abstract: Background: Hepatitis B virus (HBV) infection is a major public health problem worldwide. This study assessed knowledge, attitude and practice (KAP) towards hepatitis B virus (HBV) infection and vaccination among undergraduate students of Al-Hikmah University, Ilorin, Nigeria. Methodology: A descriptive cross-sectional survey of 426 undergraduates, selected by multistage sampling across all faculties, used a structured self-administered questionnaire. Data were analysed using descriptive statistics and chi-square tests (α = 0.05). Results: Knowledge was good overall (grand mean = 0.70; 70.1% correct), best for the viral cause (84.5%) and weakest for sexual transmission (56.1%). Attitude towards vaccination was positive (grand mean = 2.76/4.00), although cost (58.5%) and fear of side effects (69.5%) were cited as barriers. Preventive practice was adequate (3.08/4.00), but screening (2.78) lagged behind avoiding shared sharps (3.67). Knowledge (χ2(1) = 10.56, p = .001) and attitude (χ2(1) = 13.87, p < .001) were each associated with practice. Conclusion: Knowledge, attitude and practice were generally favourable, but gaps in knowledge of sexual transmission, cost and safety concerns, and low screening uptake persist. Targeted health education on transmission and improved access to vaccination and screening are recommended.

Data were analysed using descriptive statistics and chi-square tests (α = 0.05). Results: Knowledge was good overall (grand mean = 0.70; 70.1% correct), best for the viral cause (84.5%) and weakest for sexual transmission (56.1%). Attitude towards vaccination was positive (grand mean = 2.76/4.00), although cost (58.5%) and fear of side effects (69.5%) were cited as barriers. Preventive practice was adequate (3.08/4.00), but screening (2.78) lagged behind avoiding shared sharps (3.67). Knowledge (χ2(1) = 10.56, p = .001) and attitude (χ2(1) = 13.87, p < .001) were each associated with practice. Conclusion: Knowledge, attitude and practice were generally favourable, but gaps in knowledge of sexual transmission, cost and safety concerns, and low screening uptake persist. Targeted health education on transmission and improved access to vaccination and screening are recommended.

title: Knowledge, Attitudes, and Practices of Pregnant Women and Health Care Workers Regarding Antenatal Testing for HIV, Hepatitis B Virus, and Syphilis in Vietnam: Protocol for a Multicenter Cross-Sectional Study
abstract: Abstract Background Mother-to-child transmission (MTCT) of HIV, hepatitis B virus, and syphilis remains a preventable cause of fetal loss, neonatal morbidity, and long-term disability. In Vietnam (Viet Nam), although antenatal care coverage is high, gaps persist in the timing, uptake, and completion of screening and follow-up services for these infections. Objective This study has 2 parallel population-specific objectives. Among women who recently gave birth, we will estimate completion of antenatal testing for HIV, hepatitis B virus, and syphilis and its associated factors with study-defined optimal testing (completion of all 3 tests during the first trimester). Among health care workers (HCWs), we will assess knowledge, attitudes, and reported practices and identify professional factors associated with good practice regarding antenatal screening and MTCT prevention. Methods This multicenter, hospital-based cross-sectional study was conducted from June to September 2026 in 4 provincial hospitals in northern Vietnam. Women completed an interviewer-administered questionnaire after delivery, once clinically stable and before discharge. Antenatal testing was verified from maternal records, laboratory reports, or electronic records whenever available. HCWs completed a separate anonymous self-administered questionnaire during the same study period. The 2 participant groups were not matched. The primary outcome for women is completion of all 3 antenatal tests during the first trimester (study-defined optimal testing). The primary outcome for HCWs is good practice regarding the prevention of MTCT. The minimum target sample sizes were 601 women and 601 HCWs. Data will be analyzed separately for each group. Descriptive analyses will summarize knowledge, attitudes, and practices indicators and service uptake. Modified Poisson regression with robust variance will be used to identify factors independently associated with the primary outcomes. Results The protocol received ethics approval on February 9, 2026. The study is funded by Thai Binh University of Medicine and Pharmacy, Hung Yen, Vietnam. Recruitment was conducted from June to September 2026. As of manuscript submission, 601 patients and 601 health care workers had been recruited. Data cleaning is planned for October 2026, followed by statistical analysis from November to December 2026. Dissemination of the first study results is planned for the first quarter of 2027. Conclusions The study will provide hospital-based evidence on completion of antenatal triple screening and provider practices. By prespecifying distinct outcomes for women and HCWs, the study is designed to identify actionable gaps while avoiding causal interpretation of cross-sectional associations.

title: Prevalence, Microbiological Profile, and Risk Factors for Spontaneous Bacterial Peritonitis Among Cirrhotic Patients with Ascites in Africa: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
abstract: Liver cirrhosis represents the irreversible end-stage consequence of chronic hepatic inflammation and progressive fibrogenesis, accounting for more than 1.48 million deaths annually and ranking among the leading causes of premature mortality worldwide (Liu & Chen, 2022). The epidemiological burden of cirrhosis is disproportionately concentrated in Africa, particularly across sub-Saharan and North African nations, where age-standardized cirrhosis-related mortality rates remain the highest globally (Devarbhavi et al., 2026; Luo et al., 2025). Whereas alcohol-associated liver disease and metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease predominate in Western nations, cirrhosis across Africa is driven primarily by hyperendemic chronic hepatitis B virus (HBV) infection in sub-Saharan regions and historically high hepatitis C virus (HCV) seroprevalence in North Africa (Devarbhavi et al., 2023). Because structured viral hepatitis screening, antiviral therapy, and portal hypertension surveillance remain inaccessible to large segments of the African population, most patients present to tertiary referral hospitals only after transitioning from compensated cirrhosis to overt clinical decompensation (Duah & Nkrumah, 2019; Sindato et al., 2026). The development of ascites, driven by portal hypertension, splanchnic arterial vasodilation, and neurohumoral sodium and water retention, is the most frequent first decompensating event in cirrhosis (Biggins et al., 2021). Once ascites develop, patient prognosis deteriorates markedly due to superimposed bacterial infections, variceal hemorrhage, and hepatorenal syndrome (Bernardi et al., 2015; Garcia-Tsao, 2016). Globally, bacterial infections affect 35.1% of cirrhotic patients and 44.2% of those with acute-on-chronic liver failure (ACLF) (Tian et al., 2025). Spontaneous bacterial peritonitis (SBP), defined as an infection of previously sterile ascitic fluid with an ascitic polymorphonuclear (PMN) leukocyte count ≥250〖" cells/mm" 〗^3 and/or a positive monomicrobial bacterial culture without a surgical intra-abdominal source, is the most lethal infectious complication of cirrhotic ascites (Angeli et al., 2018; Biggins et al., 2021; Huang et al., 2022). Driven by pathological bacterial translocation and cirrhosis-associated immune dysfunction(Albillos et al., 2014; Wiest et al., 2014), SBP precipitates systemic inflammatory response syndrome, acute kidney injury, hepatorenal syndrome, hepatic encephalopathy, and ACLF, increasing inpatient mortality fourfold (Mahassadi et al., 2018; Miranda-Zazueta et al., 2020). Because most SBP episodes are asymptomatic at presentation (Tu et al., 2020) and every hour of delayed diagnostic paracentesis increases in-hospital mortality by 3.3% (Kim et al., 2014), outcomes remain poor in resource-limited African settings where timely paracentesis, blood-culture bottle inoculation, and human albumin infusion are often unavailable (Ajayi et al., 2013; Dia et al., 2014; Duah & Nkrumah, 2019). Despite the clinical severity of SBP in Africa, its continental epidemiology remains poorly synthesized and marked by wide discrepancies across individual studies. Previous global meta-analyses have included only two to three African studies, generating imprecise regional prevalence estimates with extremely wide confidence intervals (Tay et al., 2021; Tian et al., 2025) and have not disaggregated African microbiological profiles or multivariable risk factors. To address these critical evidence gaps, we conducted a systematic review and meta-analysis to estimate the overall prevalence of SBP in Africa, quantify the microbiological spectrum, and synthesize independent multivariable risk factors to guide clinical management.

title: From bench to bedside: 60-year development of adenine nucleoside- and nucleotide-based antiviral drugs.
abstract: SUMMARY Human pathogenic viruses, including HIV, hepatitis B virus, and hepatitis C virus, as well as recent global outbreaks and pandemics caused by RNA viruses such as severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus (SARS-CoV; 2002–2003), Middle East respiratory syndrome-CoV (2012–2015 and 2019), and SARS-CoV-2 (2019–2023), have resulted in a significant loss of life. The development of antiviral drugs has provided therapeutic options, enabling more effective treatment. With the discovery of idoxuridine, the first antiviral nucleoside approved by the U.S. Food and Drug Administration in 1963, a series of antiviral nucleosides and nucleotides has been approved worldwide over the following 60 years. These drugs, with the potential to interfere with DNA/RNA synthesis, demonstrated unique therapeutic mechanisms. In this review, we focus on adenine nucleoside and nucleotide analogs as antiviral drugs, summarizing their antiviral mechanisms across the viral life cycle, representative potent small-molecule agents with diverse scaffolds, current clinical development, and combination therapies, as well as modification strategies based on the adenosine scaffold developed over the past 60 years. In addition to the development of new antiviral agents, some adenine nucleoside and nucleotide analogs have been repurposed for new indications, and some of them, such as remdesivir, exhibit broad-spectrum antiviral activity. Through the summary of past achievements, current challenges, and available opportunities in both biology and chemistry, we hope to inspire the future development of antiviral nucleosides/nucleotides.

title: TLR2 polymorphisms and infectious disease susceptibility.
abstract: Background Toll-like receptor 2 (TLR2) is key in innate immunity; variants are linked to infectious disease susceptibility, but evidence is inconsistent and mechanisms unclear. We aimed to quantify associations between TLR2 polymorphisms and infection risk, summarise proposed mechanisms, and clinical implications. Methods Following PRISMA 2020, we searched PubMed, Scopus, and Web of Science (2015-2024). Sixteen high-quality studies (N = [insert]) were included. Pooled odds ratios (ORs) with 95% confidence intervals (CIs) used fixed-effect models when I 2 ≤ 50% and random-effects when I 2 > 50%. Dominant or recessive models were pre-specified. Subgroup analyses were by pathogen, polymorphism, and ethnicity. Mechanistic evidence was synthesised narratively, distinct from association evidence. Results TLR2 rs5743708 and rs3804099 were associated with tuberculosis (OR = 2.84, 95% CI 2.23-3.62, I 2 = 50.0%, fixed-effect), hepatitis B/C (OR = 1.92, 1.71-2.15, I 2 = 91.0%, random-effects), and bacterial meningitis (OR = 1.27, 1.01-1.59, I 2 = 28.0%, fixed-effect). Syphilis showed protection (OR = 0.46, 0.22-0.95, I 2 = 18.7%, fixed-effect; two studies). Fungal infection/talaromycosis was non-significant (OR = 1.48, 0.75-2.93, I 2 = 0.0%, fixed-effect). rs3804099 TT was linked to milder hepatitis B in individual studies. Functional studies suggest rs5743708 impairs MyD88 signaling and rs3804099 modulates IL-6, but these were not directly tested. Egger's test indicated asymmetry (intercept = 0.81, p = 0.045). Conclusions TLR2 polymorphisms show pathogen- and population-specific associations, but evidence is insufficient for diagnostic, prognostic, or therapeutic use. Associations require validation in large, multi-ethnic, prospective cohorts. Mechanistic insights from functional studies need direct validation.

title: Pooled Prevalence of Infectious Diseases Among First Responders in the Prehospital Setting: A Systematic Review With Meta-Analysis by Occupation.
abstract: OBJECTIVES: First responders often work in unpredictable, uncontrolled environments, where exposure to infected patients and contaminated environments heighten the risk of communicable disease transmission. Their higher infection prevalence compared with the general population has driven the implementation of personal protective equipment, vaccination requirements, safety protocols, and infection prevention education. The aim of this systematic review and meta-analysis was to estimate the pooled prevalence of infections among first responders in the prehospital workers including paramedics, emergency medical technicians, patient transport staff, firefighters, police, and police officers. METHODS: Embase, CINAHL, Web of Science, and PUBMED/Medline were systematically searched. Pooled prevalence estimates were calculated using random-effects models with restricted maximum likelihood estimation, with Freeman-Tukey double-arcsine transformation and back-transformation to the original prevalence scale. Heterogeneity was assessed using I2, τ2, and 95% prediction intervals. Meta-regression was used to examine potential sources of between-study heterogeneity, and small-study effects and potential publication bias were assessed using funnel plots and Egger's regression test. Risk of bias was investigated using the AXIS tool. RESULTS: Following the initial search, 34,874 articles were identified, of which 88 were full-text screened. Of these, 22 studies representing 19,188 first responders were included in this systematic review. The pooled prevalences of hepatitis B and C were 6.2% (95% CI 4.5%-8.2%) and 1.8% (95% CI 0.9%-2.9%), respectively. Around 4% (95% CI 2.6%-5.9%) of the first responders had MRSA colonization. Current or past infection with COVID-19 among non-vaccinated first responders was 13.6% (95% CI 4.8%-25.9%), which reduced to 7.3% (95% CI 3.6%-12%) after exclusion of studies with high risk of bias. Of the known study characteristics, geographic region significantly contributed to heterogeneity, explaining 36.7% of between-study variance, p = 0.039. CONCLUSIONS: Infectious disease prevalence varied across pathogens, occupations, and geographical settings among first responders. These findings should be interpreted in light of substantial heterogeneity and limitations in the available evidence but may help inform infection prevention, occupational health policy, vaccination strategies, and future research in first responder services.

title: Linked deletions in BCP and preS1 enhance HBV replication.
abstract: BACKGROUND & AIMS: Hepatitis B virus (HBV) persists as genetically heterogeneous viral populations during chronic infection, yet how linked variants and complementation among coexisting genomes shape viral phenotypes remains unclear. The BCP is a critical transcriptional control element embedded within the X open reading frame and that the preS1 region, aside from encoding a protein domain, controls the transcription of the LHBs protein. We investigated the genomic linkage and cooperative effects of disease-associated BCP and 5' preS1 deletions during chronic HBV infection. METHODS: Full-length HBV genomes from 246 treatment-naive patients with genotype B and C infection were analyzed by nanopore sequencing. Representative variants were investigated in HepG2 replication, NTCP-dependent infection and hydrodynamic-injection mouse models. RESULTS: Linked BCP-5' preS1 deletions were identified exclusively in genotype C among 3,886 full-length HBV haplotypes and were more prevalent in HBeAg-positive chronic hepatitis B (Phase II) than in HBeAg-positive chronic HBV infection (Phase I) (26% vs. Carriers had higher HBV DNA levels than non-carriers (8.57 ± 0.21 vs. 8.36 ± 0.30 log10 IU/ml; p = 0.028). Linked deletions increased extracellular HBV DNA approximately 8.0-fold relative to WT in transfected HepG2 cells. This replication advantage resulted from complementary effects of increased pgRNA production by BCP deletions and enhanced reverse transcription by the mutant Polymerase generated by the 5' preS1 deletion. However, BCP deletions also impaired productive infection through HBx truncation. HBx supplied in trans restored infectivity in cells and rescued the linked-deletion phenotype in vivo. CONCLUSIONS: Distantly linked BCP and 5' preS1 deletions cooperatively enhance HBV replication, revealing how linked variants within heterogeneous HBV populations cooperative to shape viral evolution, persistence, and pathogenicity. IMPACT AND IMPLICATIONS: HBV mutation studies have traditionally focused on individual genomic regions. However, linked variants within heterogeneous viral populations may exhibit distinct biological and clinical effects. Our findings revealed that low abundance BCP-5' preS1 deletion haplotypes can acquire enhanced replication and infection capacity through intra-genomic cooperation and inter-genomic complementation, highlighting the potential clinical relevance of minority HBV variants. Full-length haplotype based-analyses may uncover previously unrecognized cooperative viral populations that influence persistence and treatment response, warranting validation in larger longitudinal cohorts.

title: Prevalence and Associated Factors of HBsAg Positivity Among Pregnant Women Attending the Antenatal Care Clinic at Felege Hiwot Comprehensive Specialized Hospital, Bahir Dar, Northwest Ethiopia, October-December 2025: A Cross-Sectional Study.
abstract: BACKGROUND: Hepatitis B virus infection remains a major public health concern, particularly in highly endemic settings, where mother-to-child transmission is an important route of infection. This study aimed to determine the prevalence of hepatitis B surface antigen positivity and identify factors associated with HBsAg positivity among pregnant women attending antenatal care at Felege Hiwot Comprehensive Specialized Hospital in Bahir Dar, Northwest Ethiopia. METHODS: A cross-sectional study was conducted among 524 pregnant women attending the antenatal care clinic at Felege Hiwot Comprehensive Specialized Hospital from October 1 to December 30, 2025. Participants were selected using systematic random sampling. Data were collected using a structured, interviewer-administered questionnaire covering sociodemographic, obstetric, and behavioral characteristics. Five milliliters of venous blood were collected from each participant, and serum was tested for HBsAg using the SNIBE MAGLUMI chemiluminescence immunoassay. Data were entered into EpiData version 3.1 and analyzed using SPSS version 26.0. Bivariable and multivariable logistic regression analyses were performed. Variables with p < 0.25 in the bivariable analysis were considered for the multivariable model. Adjusted odds ratios (AORs) with 95% confidence intervals (CIs) were reported, and p < 0.05 was considered statistically significant. RESULTS: The prevalence of HBsAg positivity was 11.1% (58/524; 95% CI: 8.4%-13.8%). HBsAg positivity was associated with being divorced or widowed (AOR = 2.05; 95% CI: 1.02-4.13; p = 0.044), a history of sexually transmitted infection (AOR = 2.55; 95% CI: 1.38-4.71; p = 0.003), having one current sexual partner (AOR = 0.48; 95% CI: 0.26-0.87; p = 0.016), and a family history of HBV infection (AOR = 2.45; 95% CI: 1.18-5.08; p = 0.016). Only 140 participants (26.7%) reported having previously received information about HBV. CONCLUSION: HBsAg positivity was prevalent among pregnant women attending antenatal care at Felege Hiwot Comprehensive Specialized Hospital. The observed associations with marital status, STI history, number of current sexual partners, and family history of HBV infection highlight the importance of strengthening HBV screening and prevention services within antenatal care.

title: Historical, Legal and Scientific Issues of Paediatric Vaccine Mandates
abstract: This review outlines the scientific and legal foundations for a revision of the regulations concerning mandatory vaccinations, with a particular focus on the situation in Italy. The ten vaccines made mandatory by Italian Law No. 119/2017 (against poliomyelitis, diphtheria, tetanus, pertussis, hepatitis B, Haemophilus influenzae type b, measles, mumps, rubella, and varicella) are re-examined, with a particular consideration on their capacity to safeguard public health and, therefore, the interests of the community—a requirement that the Italian Constitution (Article 32) stipulates as a possible justification for mandating a medical treatment. Effects on infection, transmission, and duration of protection differ substantially between vaccines. Their implications regarding the need for vaccination—and the duration of any potential mandate for different segments of the population—must therefore be evaluated separately for each disease. While certain vaccines may be useful in specific epidemiological contexts, there is no justification for a generalized vaccination mandate for children. The analysis further indicates that scientific knowledge gained in recent years through active pharmacovigilance—some of which was not available in 2017—shows that adverse effects of vaccines on children’s health are far from negligible, especially when weighed against the low incidence of most of the infectious diseases in question. This invokes the precautionary principle, a cornerstone of medicine, together with the need for truly informed consent, grounded in real-world data.

title: Liver and spleen stiffness by 2D shear-wave elastography for identifying high-risk varices in cirrhosis: a prospective cohort study.
abstract: PURPOSE: This study evaluated the performance of liver and spleen stiffness measurement (LSM and SSM) by two-dimensional shear-wave elastography (2D-SWE) in ruling out high-risk esophageal varices (HRVs) and their utility in predicting other portal hypertension-related gastroduodenal lesions and liver-related events (LREs) in patients with cirrhosis. MATERIALS AND METHODS: This prospective cohort study enrolled consecutive adult patients with cirrhosis undergoing screening esophagogastroduodenoscopy (EGD) between 2023 and 2025 at Chulalongkorn University Hospital, Thailand. LSM and SSM were acquired using 2D-SWE (Supersonic Mach 30) within 2 days of EGD by a single blinded operator. HRVs were defined endoscopically as medium-to-large varices or small varices with red wale markings. RESULTS: 169 consecutive patients with cirrhosis were enrolled. Of these, 77 (45.6%) and 40 (23.7%) patients had esophageal varices (EVs) and HRVs, respectively. Leading cirrhosis causes were hepatitis B and C virus (n = 66, 39.1%). At thresholds to maximize specificity while maintaining sensitivity ≥ 90%, LSM < 13.7 kPa and SSM < 37.6 kPa by 2D-SWE could spare EGD in 36.7% and 44.4%, respectively, with corresponding missed HRV rates of 4.8% and 4%. Moreover, 2D-SWE-derived LSM and SSM yielded AUCs of 0.778 and 0.844 for HRVs, 0.742 and 0.785 for EVs, and 0.766 and 0.724 for portal hypertensive gastropathy (all p < 0.001). In multivariate Cox proportional hazards analysis, Child-Pugh score and LSM by 2D-SWE were independently associated with the development of LREs within 1 year. CONCLUSION: LSM and SSM using 2D-SWE may help reduce the need for screening EGD in patients with cirrhosis, with observed missed-HRV rates of 4.8% and 4.0%, respectively. These findings support further evaluation of 2D-SWE for variceal risk stratification, particularly where vibration-controlled transient elastography is unavailable. The proposed cutoffs require external validation before clinical implementation.

source_records.abstract: Purpose This study evaluated the performance of liver and spleen stiffness measurement (LSM and SSM) by two-dimensional shear-wave elastography (2D-SWE) in ruling out high-risk esophageal varices (HRVs) and their utility in predicting other portal hypertension-related gastroduodenal lesions and liver-related events (LREs) in patients with cirrhosis. Materials and methods This prospective cohort study enrolled consecutive adult patients with cirrhosis undergoing screening esophagogastroduodenoscopy (EGD) between 2023 and 2025 at Chulalongkorn University Hospital, Thailand. LSM and SSM were acquired using 2D-SWE (Supersonic Mach 30) within 2 days of EGD by a single blinded operator. HRVs were defined endoscopically as medium-to-large varices or small varices with red wale markings. Results 169 consecutive patients with cirrhosis were enrolled. Of these, 77 (45.6%) and 40 (23.7%) patients had esophageal varices (EVs) and HRVs, respectively. Leading cirrhosis causes were hepatitis B and C virus (n = 66, 39.1%). At thresholds to maximize specificity while maintaining sensitivity ≥ 90%, LSM Conclusion LSM and SSM using 2D-SWE may help reduce the need for screening EGD in patients with cirrhosis, with observed missed-HRV rates of 4.8% and 4.0%, respectively. These findings support further evaluation of 2D-SWE for variceal risk stratification, particularly where vibration-controlled transient elastography is unavailable. The proposed cutoffs require external validation before clinical implementation.

title: Targeting T follicular helper (Tfh) Cells for Improved Vaccine Efficacy: Lessons from Diverse Disease Models.
abstract: Despite remarkable progress in vaccinology, many vaccines fail to generate durable and broadly protective immunity against rapidly evolving and deadly pathogens. Conventional vaccine strategies often rely on quantifying antibody titers or neutralizing antibodies, but accumulating evidence suggests that humoral responses alone may not ensure long-term protection. An effective vaccine must engage multiple components of the immune system, harnessing intricate cellular interactions to generate durable immunological memory. Among these, CD4+ T follicular helper (Tfh) cells have emerged as central players in orchestrating germinal center (GC) dynamics, where they provide essential signals to B cells for affinity maturation, class switching, and differentiation into memory B cells and long-lived plasma cells. Tfh cells thus directly shape the magnitude and quality of vaccine-induced antibody responses. Clinical and experimental studies across infections such as influenza, HIV, HBV, and SARS-CoV-2 highlight that robust Tfh responses correlate with effective immunity and reduced disease severity. However, most licensed vaccines elicit suboptimal or short-lived Tfh activation, underscoring a critical limitation in current vaccine design. This review provides a comprehensive overview of vaccines targeting Tfh cells across various diseases, elucidating their mechanistic contributions to vaccine-induced immunity, and how their modulation could improve next-generation vaccine strategies. By harnessing Tfh biology, future vaccines could achieve durable, high-quality antibody responses, offering improved protection against emerging and re-emerging infectious diseases.

title: Reducing immunization inequities among zero-dose and under-vaccinated children through catch-up vaccination in Burkina Faso: findings from a mixed-method evaluation of the Big Catch-Up initiative implemented from 2023 to 2025
abstract: Abstract Background The COVID-19 pandemic and persistent insecurity have exacerbated inequalities in access to immunization in Burkina Faso, leading to an increase in the number of zero-dose and under-vaccinated children, particularly in hard-to-reach areas. In response, the country launched the Big Catch-Up initiative (2023–2025) to catch up children aged 12–59 months, restore immunization coverage, and strengthen routine immunization services. Six vaccines were used: measles-rubella (MR), yellow fever (YF), bivalent oral poliovirus vaccine (bOPV), meningococcal A (MenA), diphtheria-tetanus-pertussis–hepatitis B–Haemophilus influenzae type b (DTP-HepB-Hib), and inactivated poliovirus vaccine (IPV). Methods This study aimed to assess the contribution of the Big Catch-Up initiative to the vaccination of zero-dose and under-vaccinated children in Burkina Faso. We conducted a mixed-methods evaluation between November 2025 and January 2026 in six regions purposively selected based on accessibility and vaccination performance. Data were collected through direct observations and semi-structured interviews with stakeholders at the central, regional, health district, health facility, and community levels. Data collection tools were digitized using Kobo Collect, and the data were stored on the Ministry of Health’s servers. Quantitative data were analyzed using Excel and Stata. Qualitative data were reviewed and analyzed manually, coded, and organized into thematic categories. Results By December 2025, the initiative had reached 144,245 zero-dose children (65% of the target) and 200,624 under-vaccinated children (90% of the target). Improvements were observed in routine immunization indicators, particularly Penta1, Penta3, and MR2 coverage. Integrating catch-up vaccination with primary health care services facilitated access to underserved populations and enabled the delivery of complementary services, including vitamin A supplementation and deworming. Community engagement, local leadership, and service integration were key success factors. Persistent barriers included insecurity, geographical inaccessibility, population mobility, limited human resources, logistical constraints, poor Internet connectivity, and vaccine-related misinformation. Conclusions The Big Catch-Up initiative enabled zero-dose and under-vaccinated children to receive catch-up vaccinations while strengthening routine immunization. The findings also highlight the importance of integrated, community-centered, and data-driven approaches to improving equitable access to vaccination in fragile settings. Sustaining these gains will require institutionalizing catch-up vaccination within routine immunization and primary health care services, as well as implementing strategies tailored to hard-to-reach and insecure areas.
journal: International Journal for Equity in Health

title: Occupational exposures to blood and body fluids in dental care: A 14-year surveillance study using cluster analysis.
abstract: This study analyzed 14 years of occupational exposure notifications in dental settings and applied cluster analysis to identify distinct exposure profiles. The findings aim to inform targeted prevention strategies and strengthen biosafety policies in similar middle-income contexts. We analyzed 1,054 surveillance notifications recorded in the Sistema de Informação de Agravos de Notificação (SINAN) from 2006 to 2019. Variables included worker characteristics, exposure type, personal protective equipment (PPE) use, laboratory information, vaccination, and post-exposure management. Two-Step clustering was applied to identify exposure profiles. Most workers were female (85.1%) and had a university degree (64.7%). Dentists accounted for 39.3% of exposures, followed by assistants/technicians (22.5%) and students (22.4%). Percutaneous injuries predominated (86.5%), typically during procedures (70.0%) and involving sharp instruments (66.2%). Complete PPE use was recorded in 50.6%. Hepatitis B vaccination was complete in 78.2%, but post-vaccination immunity and laboratory data were frequently missing. Among tested sources: 5.0% HIV-positive; 0.9% HBsAg-positive, and 0.7% anti-HCV-positive. No seroconversions were documented in the available surveillance data. Cluster analysis identified two main profiles: a lower-risk pattern dominated by percutaneous exposures and high missing information, and a higher-risk pattern with mucosal and non-intact skin exposures, more positive or unknown sources, and less adequate PPE use. Occupational exposures in dentistry occur mainly during routine procedures and persist amid gaps in protective practices, such as the complete use of PPE and documentation. Improved biosafety adherence and follow-up may strengthen prevention, especially in a scenario of a progressive increase in the number of occupational accidents.
authors: Mauro Henrique Nogueira Guimarães de Abreu

title: B-cell and antibody responses to viral infections
abstract: B cells play central roles in adaptive immunity against viral infections by producing protective antibodies and contributing to immunological memory. However, virus- induced B-cell responses can also contribute to pathological conditions, including autoimmunity and B-cell lymphomas. Understanding both the protective and pathological aspects of B-cell responses to viral infections is essential for elucidating disease mechanisms and developing effective preventive and therapeutic strategies. In this thesis, we investigated B-cell and antibody responses to viral infections at the serological, cellular, and molecular levels, aiming to advance our understanding of antiviral immunity and virus-associated diseases and to translate these insights into vaccine and therapeutic antibody development. In Study I, we evaluated vaccination strategies against SARS-CoV-2, with a focus on effective and potentially cost-effective approaches. We found that a heterologous regimen consisting of two doses of an inactivated vaccine followed by an mRNA booster elicited IgG responses against the receptor-binding domain (RBD) and spike (S) proteins of the G614 and Omicron variants. These responses were comparable to those induced by three doses of an mRNA vaccine but higher than those induced by three doses of an inactivated vaccine. These findings highlight the benefit of an mRNA booster in enhancing antibody responses following inactivated SARS-CoV-2 vaccination. In Study II, we employed an antibody isotype-engineering strategy to develop a protective antibody against emerging SARS-CoV-2 variants of concern (VOCs) circulating during the first half of 2024. To this end, we engineered the potent monoclonal IgG antibody (SA55) into monomeric IgA1 (mIgA1), dimeric IgA1 (dIgA1), and secretory IgA1 (sIgA1) formats. Our results showed that conversion of SA55 from IgG to mIgA1 markedly enhanced its neutralizing activity against Omicron variants, including those harboring additional mutations, compared with the original IgG format, while dIgA1 and sIgA1 conferred even greater neutralizing potency. In Study III, we investigated an antigen design strategy to induce immune responses against SARS-CoV-2 and future variants. Our results showed that ancestral sequence reconstruction of coronavirus proteins can generate stable and highly soluble ancestral scaffold antigens capable of eliciting immune responses against both the wild-type (wt) RBD and circulating variants in a human immune organoid model based on tonsil cells. In Study IV, we investigated the mechanisms underlying the development of autoantibodies (autoAbs) against type I interferons (IFNs), which compromise antiviral immunity in patients with severe COVID-19 and autoimmune polyendocrine syndrome type 1 (APS-1). High-throughput autoAb profiling revealed strong autoreactivity against multiple type I IFNs and other autoantigens in patients with severe COVID-19. By combining the isolation and cloning of type I IFN-specific B cells with single-cell RNA sequencing and B-cell receptor (BCR) sequencing, we demonstrated that type I IFN autoreactivity was present in both naïve and antigen-experienced B-cell compartments, whereas functional IFN- neutralizing antibodies were predominantly associated with memory and atypical B-cell subsets. In Study V, we sought to understand the mechanisms underlying lymphomagenesis in hepatitis B virus (HBV)-associated diffuse large B-cell lymphoma (DLBCL), focusing on the antigen reactivity of tumor-derived BCRs. We found that a subset of dominant tumor BCRs recognized HBV surface and core antigens and frequently exhibited broad autoreactivity against diverse autoimmunity-associated antigens. These findings suggest a potential mechanistic link between HBV infection, autoreactivity, and lymphomagenesis. In conclusion, this thesis provides comprehensive insights into B-cell biology and antibody responses in protective antiviral immunity, autoimmunity, and B-cell lymphoma. By characterizing B-cell responses, particularly BCR specificities and their functional properties, across healthy and disease contexts, our findings advance our understanding of virus-associated immunity and immunopathology and provide a foundation for developing antibody-based therapeutics and vaccines. title: Serial Endoscopic Variceal Band Ligation for Esophageal Varices Due to Portal Hypertension: A Prospective Observational Study from Southern Rajasthan
abstract: Abstract Background Esophageal variceal hemorrhage is a major decompensating event in portal hypertension. Endoscopic variceal band ligation (EVBL) controls bleeding by mechanically strangulating varices while avoiding the deeper tissue injury associated with sclerosant injection. Although EVBL is established in acute hemostasis and secondary prevention, the number of sessions required for eradication and the practical pattern of short-term adverse effects may vary with disease severity, referral pathways, and follow-up adherence. This study evaluated serial EVBL in adults treated at a tertiary-care hospital in Udaipur, Rajasthan. Methods This hospital-based prospective observational study included 40 adults with portal hypertension and esophageal varices who underwent EVBL at the American International Institute of Medical Sciences between April 2023 and March 2025. Participants were assessed clinically and with routine laboratory testing and abdominal imaging when indicated. Upper gastrointestinal endoscopy was repeated at four-week intervals, with further EVBL until complete variceal obliteration. Outcomes were summarized using frequencies, proportions, and means. The principal outcomes were number of sessions to obliteration, change in endoscopic grade, recurrence at six months, and procedure-related adverse effects. Results The participants were 31 men and 9 women, aged 31–80 years. Hematemesis was the leading presenting complaint in 20 patients (50.0%), followed by melena in 10 (25.0%). Cirrhosis was the recorded cause of portal hypertension in 31 patients; the reported etiologic distribution was alcohol-associated disease in 21 (52.5% of the cohort), chronic hepatitis B in 11 (27.5%), and non-alcoholic fatty liver disease in 8 (20.0%). Twenty-six patients (64.0%) were Child–Pugh class A, 12 (30.0%) class B, and 2 (6.0%) class C. At baseline, 10 patients had grade I, 16 grade II, and 14 grade III varices. Five patients achieved obliteration by eight weeks and 35 by 12 weeks; the mean number of sessions was 2.875. At six-month endoscopy, 25 patients returned: 18 had no reappearance and 7 underwent repeat EVBL for recurrent varices. Retrosternal pain occurred in 12 patients (30.0%), fever in 4 (10.0%), and hematemesis in 2 (5.0%); no stricture was recorded. Conclusions In this single-centre cohort, serial EVBL achieved documented obliteration in two or three sessions for all patients who completed the eradication protocol, with mostly transient adverse effects. The six-month assessment was limited by loss to follow-up, and recurrence among reviewed patients supports continued surveillance. The findings support a pragmatic four-week EVBL pathway but should not be interpreted as comparative evidence of superiority over pharmacological or shunt-based strategies.

title: Clinical Significance of Indeterminate Antibody to Hepatitis C in Cancer Patients.
abstract: Most patients with cancer are screened for hepatitis C virus (HCV) infection using an antibody to HCV (anti-HCV) test. However, the importance of an indeterminate anti-HCV result is unknown. We investigated the clinical significance of an indeterminate anti-HCV result in cancer patients. We conducted a retrospective cohort study of cancer patients screened for HCV infection using ARCHITECT Anti-HCV at our institution between October 2016 and July 2024. Patients were categorized based on their anti-HCV results as patients with indeterminate anti-HCV and undetectable HCV-RNA in the absence of HCV treatment, and patients with reactive anti-HCV and chronic infection. We compared the two groups using univariable analyses and multivariable logistic regression analysis. Of the 112,180 patients screened with anti-HCV, 114 (0.1%) had indeterminate results; 101 of them with confirmed cancer were further analysed. Anti-HCV testing was repeated in 24 (24%) patients; most (84%) had non-reactive (46%) or indeterminate (38%) results. Among the 101 patients with indeterminate anti-HCV, 98 (97%) did not have proven HCV infection, but 3 (3%) had HCV infection. Multivariable analysis showed that male sex (adjusted odds ratio [aOR] 2.22, 95% confidence interval [CI] 1.40-3.53, p < 0.001), age ≥ 60 years (aOR 1.61, 95% CI 1.01-2.56, p = 0.046), hepatitis B or HIV coinfection (aOR 3.13, 95% CI 1.21-8.11, p = 0.019) and cirrhosis (aOR 6.67, 95% CI 2.05-21.69, p = 0.002) were more likely to have chronic than an indeterminate anti-HCV result. Indeterminate anti-HCV results are uncommon in cancer patients and rarely indicate HCV infection.

title: Burden and risk factors of HBV, HCV, syphilis, and HIV infections among homeless patients with severe mental illness: a retrospective comparative study in Southern China
abstract: People experiencing homelessness and severe mental illness face barriers to prevention, timely diagnosis, and longitudinal care for blood-borne and sexually transmitted infections. This study examined the serological burden of four pathogens and associated behavioral, nutritional, and clinical factors among psychiatric inpatients. We evaluated 470 psychiatric inpatients admitted between January 2020 and January 2024, comprising 235 homeless patients and 235 age- and sex-matched non-homeless controls. Admission screening comprised hepatitis B surface antigen (HBsAg), anti-HCV, treponemal antibody, and anti-HIV. Paired comparisons used two-sided exact McNemar tests. Associations with positivity for at least one screening marker were assessed using univariable and multivariable logistic regression; discrimination, calibration, and collinearity were evaluated. CD4 + T-cell counts were analyzed with adjustment for HIV screening status and relevant covariates. HBsAg, anti-HCV, treponemal-antibody, and anti-HIV positivity were 29/235 (12.3%) versus 18/235 (7.7%), 26/235 (11.1%) versus 9/235 (3.8%), 17/235 (7.2%) versus 5/235 (2.1%), and 7/235 (3.0%) versus 2/235 (0.9%) in homeless and control groups, respectively. Anti-HCV ( P = 0.003) and treponemal-antibody ( P = 0.017) comparisons were statistically significant. Any marker was reactive in 69/235 (29.4%) versus 31/235 (13.2%; P 3 years (adjusted OR 6.61, 95% CI 2.89–15.13), injection drug use (12.86, 5.52–29.95), and unprotected sexual behavior (3.29, 1.52–7.14) were associated with combined seroreactivity. Apparent AUC was 0.848, and the optimism-corrected AUC was 0.827 (bootstrap 95% CI 0.766–0.882). Homeless psychiatric inpatients had higher anti-HCV and treponemal-antibody reactivity and an elevated combined burden of positive infection screening markers. Social instability, behavioral exposures, psychiatric treatment continuity, and nutritional vulnerability may inform risk assessment and coordinated care. Confirmation of infection and prospective evaluation of integrated service models remain essential.

title: A novel role of NOX2 in enhancing HBV replication through ROS‐mediated autophagy activation
abstract: Hepatitis B virus (HBV) is a serious global public health issue. Mounting evidence suggests that NADPH oxidase 2 (NOX2) plays critical roles in various physiological and pathological processes. However, the underlying mechanisms by which NOX2 affects HBV infection remain to be elucidated. In the present study, the potential role of NOX2 in HBV replication was investigated in cell models. First, it was demonstrated that NOX2 is highly expressed in transiently and stably HBV‐infected cells. Second, by employing inhibitor, RNA interference technique and plasmid overexpression, it was revealed that NOX2 plays an essential role in promoting HBV replication. Furthermore, the underlying mechanism of how NOX2 affects HBV replication was illustrated. It was found that NOX2‐mediated ROS induce an increase of intracellular autophagy levels, which result in facilitating HBV replication. These results suggested a previously unrecognized role of NOX2 in HBV replication. Taken together, NOX2 may serve as a novel target for developing treatment strategies against HBV‐related disorders.

title: The Nucleoside Analogue NITD008, Alone or Combined With Ribavirin, Potently Reduces Hepatitis E Virus Infection in Humanised Mice.
abstract: Background and aims Hepatitis E virus (HEV) infection is becoming increasingly clinically relevant worldwide, but no approved antiviral therapy currently exists. Ribavirin (RBV) is used off-label for immunosuppressed patients with chronic hepatitis E, although it is effective in only 80% of patients and linked to side effects. The nucleoside analogue NITD008 was shown to be effective against a broad range of RNA viruses. We aimed to evaluate the efficacy of NITD008, alone or in combination with RBV, in humanised mice stably infected with HEV. Methods Mice received either NITD008 alone (20 mg/Kg/day) by oral gavage for up to 2 weeks, or 5 mg/Kg NITD008 alone or in combination with RBV (50 mg/Kg). Viral changes were determined in faeces, blood and intrahepatically. Results NITD008 efficiently reduced HEV loads to undetectable levels in serum and by > 4log 10 in faeces within 1 week. Intrahepatic analysis showed a ∆log 10 : 2.5 reduction in HEV RNA levels in treated mice compared to controls after 2 weeks. Imaging showed fewer HEV-RNA-positive human hepatocytes in treated mice. NITD008 did not increase serum markers of hepatocyte death. Combination therapy induced stronger suppression of HEV RNA in faeces (∆log 10 : 5.02) than RBV monotherapy (∆log 10 : 1.08), despite lower NITD008 doses. Conclusions This study demonstrates the non-toxicity of NITD008 towards human hepatocytes and more potent antiviral activity compared to RBV in HEV-infected mice. Combination regimens with RBV showed strong additive activity. The study suggests that HEV clearance may be achieved in immunosuppressed patients by using and further developing this class of direct antiviral drugs.

source_records.title: The Nucleoside Analogue NITD008, Alone or Combined With Ribavirin, Potently Reduces Hepatitis E Virus Infection in Humanised Mice.
source_records.abstract: Background and aims Hepatitis E virus (HEV) infection is becoming increasingly clinically relevant worldwide, but no approved antiviral therapy currently exists. Ribavirin (RBV) is used off-label for immunosuppressed patients with chronic hepatitis E, although it is effective in only 80% of patients and linked to side effects. The nucleoside analogue NITD008 was shown to be effective against a broad range of RNA viruses. We aimed to evaluate the efficacy of NITD008, alone or in combination with RBV, in humanised mice stably infected with HEV. Methods Mice received either NITD008 alone (20 mg/Kg/day) by oral gavage for up to 2 weeks, or 5 mg/Kg NITD008 alone or in combination with RBV (50 mg/Kg). Combination therapy induced stronger suppression of HEV RNA in faeces (∆log 10 : 5.02) than RBV monotherapy (∆log 10 : 1.08), despite lower NITD008 doses. title: Pro/Ala/Ser (PAS) peptides as an alternative to polyethylene glycol (PEG) for the surface shielding of lipid nanoparticles (LNPs) carrying therapeutic mRNA
abstract: Abstract Lipid nanoparticles (LNPs), comprising a mixture of cationic lipids, neutral phospholipids, cholesterol and, in particular, polyethylene glycol (PEG)-conjugated lipids on their surface, have emerged as a powerful technology to encapsulate and deliver protein-encoding mRNAs as modern vaccines or for therapeutic intervention. However, the common use of PEG for surface shielding of mRNA-LNPs has raised concerns, especially in the light of a growing prevalence of anti-PEG antibodies in the healthy population. PASylation offers a biological alternative to the chemical PEG polymer, employing recombinant or synthetic (poly)peptides made of the small natural L-amino acids Pro, Ala and Ser which, in contrast to PEG, are biodegradable. PAS sequences are conformationally disordered, fully uncharged but strongly solvated and, thus, closely match the biophysical properties of PEG chains. Based on this notion, we synthesized a novel PASylated lipid, Pga-PAS 40 -ditetradecylamine (PAS-DTA), by replacing the PEG moiety in a clinically approved PEG-lipid (ALC-0159) with a 40mer PAS peptide N-terminally protected with pyroglutamate (Pga). mRNA-LNPs were formulated with this PASylated lipid, adopting a published procedure for conventional LNPs, and their properties were compared with those prepared using common PEG-lipids. To this end, we designed template DNAs for the in vitro transcription (IVT) of mRNA encoding a PASylated murine interferon alpha-11 (mIFNα11) which, when systemically applied, is effective against hepatitis B infection of transgenic mice. mRNA-LNPs formulated with PASylated or PEGylated lipids showed practically identical RNA-encapsulation efficiencies (~ 50%), hydrodynamic diameters (85–120 nm) as well as Zeta potentials (− 4 to − 13 mV). In addition, cultured HepG2 and HEK293E cells transfected with the PASylated mRNA-LNPs encoding either enhanced green fluorescent protein (eGFP) or PAS 200 -mIFNα11 showed robust expression of both recombinant proteins. Furthermore, in a side-by-side experiment with HepG2 cells transfected with mRNA-LNPs that were prepared using PAS-DTA or two different PEG-lipids, comparable or slightly higher amounts of secreted PAS 200 -mIFNα11 were detected in the culture supernatant both by western blotting and ELISA. Taken together, our in vitro data indicate that PAS-lipids offer a viable alternative to PEG-lipids for the preparation of mRNA-LNPs, without immunochemical cross-reactivity but with potentially better tolerability for the transfected target cells.

title: Cabozantinib Could Inhibit Hepatitis A Virus Replication in Human Hepatoma Cell Lines
abstract: Background/Objectives: Tyrosine kinase inhibitors (TKIs) have been reported to suppress the replication of several hepatotropic viruses. Despite being preventable through vaccination, hepatitis A virus (HAV) infection is still a worldwide public health issue and is also prevalent in Japan. In the context of Japan’s aging population, it is expected that the number of patients with severe hepatitis A will increase. Therefore, it is important to develop antiviral agents against HAV as therapeutic options for severe hepatitis A. Methods: In the present study, the effects of several anticancer drugs on HAV replication were examined in human hepatoma cell lines, including TKIs, which are currently used to treat patients with hepatocellular carcinoma. Results: A 48 h treatment of cabozantinib effectively inhibited HAV HA11-1299 genotype IIIA replication, and a 24 h treatment of cabozantinib with an IC50 of 3.1 μM inhibited replication of the HAV HM175-18f genotype IB subgenomic replicon. Conclusions: Cabozantinib could inhibit HAV replication in vitro and may be useful for the drug development for HAV infection.

title: [Screening, diagnosis, treatment, and follow-up of hepatitis C virus-related liver disease].
abstract: Hepatitis C viral (HCV) infection has become curable. Eradication of the virus is essential from individual as well as from social aspects. Treatment in Hungary is based on a national consensus guideline, updated six-monthly. If there is no contraindication, demonstration of viral replication is the indication of therapy. Only direct-acting antiviral therapies are to be applied. At the time of publication of this guideline, only pan-genotypic combinations are available in Hungary. Based on fibrosis stage and on other (clinical, epidemiological, occupational, etc.) factors, a treatment prioritization system is available - however, all diagnosed infected individuals have access to reimbursed therapy nowadays. All infected individuals should be diagnosed and treated in a timely manner. 2026; 167(46): 1847-1861.

title: Streamlining Hepatitis C Treatment: Implementation of a Clinical Pharmacist-Driven Medication Management Program.
abstract: Background Hepatitis C virus (HCV) affects over 3.9 million individuals in the United States and is effectively treated with direct-acting antiviral (DAA) agents. Clinical pharmacists (CPs) may be the ideal provider to bridge gaps in HCV care by selecting appropriate therapy following drug-drug interaction (DDI) review, navigating access barriers, and supporting adherence. Although CP involvement in HCV care has demonstrated clinical value, there is limited literature describing CP workflows, patient interventions, and CP-led programs that support patients from treatment initiation through sustained virologic response at 12 weeks (SVR12). This study aims to quantify and categorize CP-driven enrollments in a Hepatitis C Clinical Program (HCCP) and assess its impact on patient safety, operational, and clinical outcomes. Methods This retrospective descriptive study evaluates a CP-driven HCCP within a health system specialty pharmacy (HSSP) from May 6, 2024 to March 6, 2025. Patients with a referral to the CP for HCV treatment selection, or external patients with a DAA claim at the HSSP, were eligible for enrollment in the program. The HCCP consisted of six points of clinical care: CP therapy selection, medication access and order placement, prescription triage and patient education, follow-up throughout treatment, intervention support, and laboratory monitoring through SVR12. Results A total of 122 patients were enrolled in the HCCP. Most patients were treatment-naïve (90%) and non-cirrhotic (79%). DDIs were identified in 57% of patients, with statin therapy being the most common (46%). Time-to-treatment was 4 days or less for 76% of patients, with an 88% HSSP prescription capture rate. A 97% SVR12 rate was achieved, and 92% of patients completed therapy on time. Conclusion This study highlights the role of the CP in HCV care and their impact on patient safety and clinical and operational outcomes. Results support further development of CP-driven practice changes and support the implementation of a similar program within other HSSPs.

title: Reductions in Advanced Chronic Liver Disease Among People Who Inject Drugs: The ETHOS Engage Study.
abstract: Background and aims Liver disease is a significant risk for people who inject drugs due to the high burden of hepatitis C virus (HCV). There is limited data on the impact of the direct-acting antiviral (DAA) therapy era on liver disease among people who inject drugs. This study evaluated baseline and longitudinal liver disease in a national cohort of people who inject drugs recruited over three Waves: 2018-2019, 2019-2021, and 2023-2025. Methods The ETHOS Engage Study is an observational cohort of people who inject drugs attending drug treatment clinics and needle and syringe programs in Australia. Participants completed a questionnaire and underwent point-of-care HCV RNA testing (Xpert HCV Viral Load Fingerstick) and liver stiffness measurement (LSM) by vibration-controlled transient hepatic elastography (FibroScan). Advanced chronic liver disease was defined by LSM of 10 kPa or above. Results Among all enrolments with a valid LSM (n = 3126, 79% recruited at drug treatment clinics), 11% had advanced chronic liver disease, decreasing from 12.0% (154/1287) in 2018-2019 to 7.9% (66/839) in 2019-2021, and 6.4% (62/967) in 2023-2025. In adjusted analyses, participants recruited between 2019-2021 and 2023-2025 were less likely to have advanced chronic liver disease (vs. 2018-2019; aOR 0.66, 95% CI: 0.48-0.90 and aOR 0.56, 95% CI: 0.40-0.77, respectively). Current HCV infection declined from 24% in 2018-2019 to 10% in 2023-2025. Among participants with LSM in more than one wave and current HCV infection at first visit and no current HCV infection at second visit (n = 44), advanced chronic liver disease declined from 19% to 5%. Conclusions Unrestricted access to DAA therapies in Australia has been associated with reduced liver disease burden among people who inject drugs. Monitoring of liver health in this population is important, given potential ageing and non-HCV liver disease impacts.

This study evaluated baseline and longitudinal liver disease in a national cohort of people who inject drugs recruited over three Waves: 2018-2019, 2019-2021, and 2023-2025. Methods The ETHOS Engage Study is an observational cohort of people who inject drugs attending drug treatment clinics and needle and syringe programs in Australia. Participants completed a questionnaire and underwent point-of-care HCV RNA testing (Xpert HCV Viral Load Fingerstick) and liver stiffness measurement (LSM) by vibration-controlled transient hepatic elastography (FibroScan). Advanced chronic liver disease was defined by LSM of 10 kPa or above. Results Among all enrolments with a valid LSM (n = 3126, 79% recruited at drug treatment clinics), 11% had advanced chronic liver disease, decreasing from 12.0% (154/1287) in 2018-2019 to 7.9% (66/839) in 2019-2021, and 6.4% (62/967) in 2023-2025. In adjusted analyses, participants recruited between 2019-2021 and 2023-2025 were less likely to have advanced chronic liver disease (vs. 2018-2019; aOR 0.66, 95% CI: 0.48-0.90 and aOR 0.56, 95% CI: 0.40-0.77, respectively). Current HCV infection declined from 24% in 2018-2019 to 10% in 2023-2025. Among participants with LSM in more than one wave and current HCV infection at first visit and no current HCV infection at second visit (n = 44), advanced chronic liver disease declined from 19% to 5%. Conclusions Unrestricted access to DAA therapies in Australia has been associated with reduced liver disease burden among people who inject drugs. Monitoring of liver health in this population is important, given potential ageing and non-HCV liver disease impacts.

title: An integrated clinical risk scoring and machine learning framework for risk stratification of hepatocellular carcinoma: Development and real-world clinical validation
abstract: Introduction: Hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) remains a major cause of cancer-related mortality, highlighting the need for more accurate risk stratification approaches. Objective: To develop and validate an integrated clinical risk scoring (CRS) and machine learning (ML) system to accurately identify HCC, overcoming the limitations of traditional alpha-fetoprotein (AFP) screening, especially in AFP-negative individuals. Methods: A retrospective cross-sectional diagnostic study utilized data from two institutions (development cohort n = 5,000; external validation cohort n = 443) with 12 routine clinical variables. Multivariable logistic regression was used to construct the CRS, and ensemble ML models were developed. Performance was assessed via area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC), quantitative calibration measures, decision curve analysis (DCA), net reclassification improvement (NRI), and integrated discrimination improvement (IDI). We applied development-trained models directly to the independent cohort for strict external validation. Results: Hepatitis C, diabetes and hepatitis B were identified as the strongest independent risk factors for HCC. In the development cohort, the CatBoost model demonstrated the best overall discriminatory ability (AUC = 0.9773), significantly outperforming the single AFP indicator (0.6377) and CRS (0.9385); notably, in the independent validation cohort, CRS demonstrated superior stability in terms of AUC (0.9849) and risk reclassification ability (NRI/IDI), performing slightly better than CatBoost (AUC = 0.9816). DCA, NRI, and IDI confirmed significant incremental clinical net benefit and risk reclassification over AFP-only screening (p < 0.001). Conclusion: This integrated HCC risk stratification system effectively overcomes traditional AFP screening limitations, particularly in AFP-negative populations. The observed bias-variance trade-off supports a tiered deployment strategy: CRS for robust screening in resource-limited settings, and ML for precision assessment in well-resourced centers.

title: Editorial: Strategies to improve awareness and management of cancer risk factors and screenings
abstract: early warning signs of cancer appears to be insufficient. Public knowledge about cancer is important because 44% of cancer deaths are attributable to modifiable risk factors (3) and because patients diagnosed at an early stage have better treatment outcomes (4). The study by Sauer et al. (5) assessed the behaviors, attitudes, and awareness regarding skin cancer among Polish medical and non-medical students. The students' knowledge of skin cancer, selfexamination, and sun protection was adequate. However, medical students demonstrated a higher level of knowledge than non-medical students. Women were more likely to use sunscreen than men. Knowledge scores correlated significantly with sunscreen use. (6) showed that education was highly effective in improving students' knowledge of melanoma prevention and recognition. The authors introduced web-based e-learning tools and peer education among high school students aged 14-16 years. Students completed pre-and post-intervention questionnaires. Knowledge of the ABCDE rule rose from 7.5% to 96.6%, and knowledge of the ugly duckling sign rose from 9.1% to 91.2%. In an international study of almost 1,000 students, Bordakiewicz et al. (7) found that young people were aware of common cancer risk factors (cigarette smoking, alcohol consumption, sunbathing or tanning bed use, exposure to ionizing radiation, diet, and occupational exposure to carcinogens). However, there were gaps in knowledge of other risk factors, such as low physical activity, viral infections, and hormonal contraception. Notably, the students overestimated the role of genetic factors. As in the study by Sauer et al. (5), medical students in this study demonstrated more accurate knowledge about cancer than non-medical students. Additionally, students with a family history of cancer knew more about cancer than those without such a history.Better-educated people are more likely to pay attention to their own health, perform selfexamination, and participate in screening. The study by Garai et al. (8) showed that half of the female students performed breast self-examination. Students with better knowledge of breast cancer prevention were more likely to practice breast self-examination. Information from gynecologists and family members played a crucial role in adherence to breast selfexamination. A family history of breast cancer was significantly associated with practicing breast self-examination. Higher self-efficacy was also an important factor in this study. In a study by Jiang et al. (9), better knowledge was associated with more positive attitudes toward human papillomavirus (HPV) vaccination. The authors showed that patients who were younger, lived in urban areas, had higher levels of education and income, and had better knowledge of cervical cancer and HPV were more willing to be vaccinated. However, of the more than 1,000 women studied, only 28% had been vaccinated. Similarly, in the study by Kandasamy et al. (10), only 21% of the women surveyed in Saudi Arabia had been vaccinated against HPV.Overall, 66% of the participants demonstrated good knowledge of HPV and cervical cancer prevention. Nevertheless, the women surveyed were not familiar with cervical cancer screening and did not participate in it regularly. The authors identified lack of knowledge and discomfort as the main barriers to undergoing a Pap test. Women who were older, less educated, or unmarried had less knowledge and more negative attitudes toward gynecological examination.Identifying effective ways to encourage participation in screening is therefore essential. (11) conducted a qualitative study to assess participants' attitudes and preferences regarding screening, using kidney cancer as an example. Patients prioritized test accuracy but also preferred procedures that were convenient, safe, non-invasive, and minimally painful. The results indicated that factors motivating patients to participate in cancer screening included health needs, social support, risk awareness, recommendations from authoritative sources, and the availability of screening. Physicians were perceived as the best and most reliable source of information; despite having access to other sources, patients still trusted physicians the most. this analysis, the authors emphasized the need for a comprehensive and region-specific approach to breast cancer control. This effort should focus on improving access to screening and advanced treatment in less developed regions, implementing tailored prevention strategies, and addressing significant modifiable risk factors, such as an unhealthy diet, a sedentary lifestyle, and obesity. (15) performed a similar analysis of GBD 2021 data for laryngeal cancer. Although the incidence of laryngeal cancer, unlike that of breast cancer, has been steadily declining, the authors emphasized the need to focus on groups that are particularly susceptible to this cancer. Cigarette smokers, as well as men younger than 75 years and those older than 85 years, should be targeted as key groups for prevention and closer surveillance.The results of these two analyses underscore the urgent need to develop global and regional public health strategies and policies regarding cancer prevention and screening.With advances in science and technology, artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly being used in oncology. ( 16) presented a narrative review that comprehensively explored the potential of AI in raising awareness about cancer risk and in managing screening programs. One area of application is the use of AI to estimate an individual's cancer risk based on their characteristics, such as genetic factors, lifestyle, exposure to carcinogens, and medical history.AI enables the integration of data from various sources, such as individual medical records and population-based cancer registries. This can help with planning preventive, informational, and educational initiatives, as well as with designing new screening programs. Digital analysis of medical images and the identification of multidimensional relationships between various features may prove to be very useful in oncology. For example, AI significantly improved the accuracy of liver cancer risk prediction in patients with chronic hepatitis B (16). Studies haveshown that ChatGPT has significant potential for automating the delivery of information on prevention and screening to patients and that it can improve both the quality of patient education and the knowledge that patients acquire. The integration of AI into national and regional screening programs can help optimize their reach and effectiveness. In the future, further progress in this field will depend on multidisciplinary collaboration: physicians, AI researchers, public health experts, and governments must work together. With this approach, AI could help reduce the global burden of cancer. However, for many people, particularly older adults, using modern technologies remains challenging. A pilot study by Ahmed et al. (17) showed that a cancer prevention mobile app tested in six European countries could raise cancer awareness, although its usefulness was rated as moderate. Technical problems were the main reason for discontinuing use of the app.The collection of articles published in this Research Topic, "Strategies to improve awareness and management of cancer risk factors and screenings," suggests that education is essential to reducing the impact of cancer on people's lives. Identifying and reaching the appropriate age and sociodemographic groups is particularly important for reducing exposure to cancer risk factors and encouraging participation in screening programs. Technological advancements, including AI, offer new global and institutional opportunities, but individuals often prefer personal contact with a physician. Physicians remain patients' primary and preferred source of information.

Although the incidence of laryngeal cancer, unlike that of breast cancer, has been steadily declining, the authors emphasized the need to focus on groups that are particularly susceptible to this cancer. Cigarette smokers, as well as men younger than 75 years and those older than 85 years, should be targeted as key groups for prevention and closer surveillance.The results of these two analyses underscore the urgent need to develop global and regional public health strategies and policies regarding cancer prevention and screening.With advances in science and technology, artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly being used in oncology. ( 16) presented a narrative review that comprehensively explored the potential of AI in raising awareness about cancer risk and in managing screening programs. One area of application is the use of AI to estimate an individual's cancer risk based on their characteristics, such as genetic factors, lifestyle, exposure to carcinogens, and medical history.AI enables the integration of data from various sources, such as individual medical records and population-based cancer registries. This can help with planning preventive, informational, and educational initiatives, as well as with designing new screening programs. Digital analysis of medical images and the identification of multidimensional relationships between various features may prove to be very useful in oncology. For example, AI significantly improved the accuracy of liver cancer risk prediction in patients with chronic hepatitis B (16). Studies haveshown that ChatGPT has significant potential for automating the delivery of information on prevention and screening to patients and that it can improve both the quality of patient education and the knowledge that patients acquire. The integration of AI into national and regional screening programs can help optimize their reach and effectiveness. In the future, further progress in this field will depend on multidisciplinary collaboration: physicians, AI researchers, public health experts, and governments must work together. With this approach, AI could help reduce the global burden of cancer. However, for many people, particularly older adults, using modern technologies remains challenging. A pilot study by Ahmed et al. (17) showed that a cancer prevention mobile app tested in six European countries could raise cancer awareness, although its usefulness was rated as moderate. Technical problems were the main reason for discontinuing use of the app.The collection of articles published in this Research Topic, "Strategies to improve awareness and management of cancer risk factors and screenings," suggests that education is essential to reducing the impact of cancer on people's lives. Identifying and reaching the appropriate age and sociodemographic groups is particularly important for reducing exposure to cancer risk factors and encouraging participation in screening programs. Technological advancements, including AI, offer new global and institutional opportunities, but individuals often prefer personal contact with a physician. Physicians remain patients' primary and preferred source of information.

title: Identification of coding-region mutations associated with attenuation of an Egyptian duck hepatitis A virus type 1 isolate following serial egg passage
abstract: Abstract Background Duck hepatitis A virus type 1 (DHAV-1) causes a highly contagious disease with high mortality in young ducklings. Although serial passage in embryonated eggs is widely used for virus adaptation and attenuation, the molecular changes associated with DHAV-1 attenuation remain poorly understood. Method A virulent Egyptian DHAV-1 isolate was serially passaged 84 times in embryonated chicken eggs. The parental virus (P0) and the passage-84 virus (P84) were subsequently compared for pathogenicity in Pekin ducklings, replication in embryonated chicken eggs, and whole-genome sequence analysis. Results The parental virus caused 100% mortality within 72 h, whereas the P84 virus caused neither clinical signs nor mortality and replicated to higher titers in embryonated chicken eggs, demonstrating complete attenuation. Whole-genome sequencing identified 11 nucleotide substitutions, including four non-synonymous mutations in the VP3, 2A, and 2C proteins. Conclusions Serial passage in embryonated chicken eggs resulted in complete attenuation of DHAV-1 after 84 passages, despite the accumulation of four amino acid substitutions. These findings demonstrate that profound phenotypic attenuation can arise with minimal genomic evolution and identify candidate mutations in VP3, 2A, and particularly 2C for future reverse-genetics studies and rational live vaccine development.

title: Real-World Effectiveness and Safety of Sofosbuvir-Based Therapy in Chinese Children and Adolescents With Chronic HCV Infection: A Retrospective Multicentre Study.
abstract: Few direct-acting antiviral regimens are approved in China for children and adolescents with chronic hepatitis C virus (HCV) infection and data are limited on their efficacy and safety in this population. This retrospective, multi-centre study aimed to assess the real-world effectiveness and safety of ledipasvir/sofosbuvir (LDV/SOF) and sofosbuvir/velpatasvir (SOF/VEL) in Chinese paediatric patients. The study included patients aged 3-17 years from five hospitals across China who received either LDV/SOF or SOF/VEL for chronic HCV infection. The outcomes included the proportion of patients who achieved sustained virologic response at 12 weeks post-treatment (SVR12), normalisation rates of ALT and AST levels, and incidence of adverse events (AEs). A total of 129 patients from five sites were included and 128 completed 12 weeks of post-treatment follow-up. Mean age was 9.9 years (standard deviation, 3.9), with 30 (23.3%), 55 (42.6%), and 44 (34.1%) patients aged 3-6, 7-11, and 12-17 years, respectively, 84 (65.1%) were male, 62 (48.1%) were infected with genotype 3, and baseline ALT and AST levels were elevated in 64 (49.6%) and 75 (58.1%) patients, respectively. The SVR12 rate was 98.4% (126/128) in the overall population, remaining consistent across subgroups by sex, age, HCV genotype, or regimen. ALT and AST levels were normalised in all patients with available data. AEs were reported by 16.4% (21/128) of patients and none were serious. Collectively, this study demonstrated that LDV/SOF and SOF/VEL were highly effective and well tolerated in Chinese paediatric patients with chronic HCV infection.
